extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of humor/creativity studies; comedy writers analyzing joke structure
extracted.subtask_description: A framework for analyzing or composing jokes by creating a moment where one element legitimately belongs to two self-consistent but normally incompatible frames (matrices), producing a sudden reinterpretation and an emotional discharge. Emphasizes matrix coherence, incompatibility, unmistakable double-fitting, sudden shift, and self-assertive emotional discharge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bisociation (defining formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: A creative act is the simultaneous perception of one event/idea/situation in two associative contexts that are normally incompatible; the two matrices intersect at the bisociative point where the same element belongs to both M1 and M2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bisociation as the core mechanism: craft an element that genuinely fits two distinct associative contexts. The bisociative point is the locus of creativity/humor — ensure the audience can perceive the double membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrix definition (what a "matrix" is)
rubrics_metrics.description: A matrix is any ability, habit, or skill, any pattern of ordered behaviour governed by a 'code' of fixed rules (e.g., mathematical reasoning, etiquette, narrative genres, domain expertise, cultural scripts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or analyzing jokes, explicitly identify the internal logic, vocabulary, expectations, and modes of relevance for each matrix (M1 and M2). Provide concrete examples to make each matrix salient to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of a joke (setup → punch → bisociation → discharge)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. Setup primes M1 — a single matrix is established. 2. Audience progresses inside M1 interpreting events according to its rules. 3. Punch line is a stimulus that also fits M2 (hidden/unexpected). 4. Sudden bisociative perception — the audience sees the same element belongs to both matrices. 5. M2 supplants M1 retroactively. 6. Discharge of laughter occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the sequence: firmly establish M1, avoid pre-revealing M2, design the punch so it is interpretable in M2 as well, and allow the retroactive reinterpretation to occur quickly so emotional energy can discharge as laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two matrices must each be internally coherent
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of the two matrices involved in the bisociation must be internally coherent; a joke that just fails inside one matrix is not funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure both frames have clear, plausible rules and expectations for the audience; avoid relying on a matrix that is ill-defined or broken-for-effect, because that weakens the bisociative surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: The two matrices must be habitually incompatible
rubrics_metrics.description: The two matrices must be habitually incompatible; if the bisociation is too easy or expected, there is no surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose matrices that the audience normally keeps separate (different domains, logics, or scripts). If the connection is too familiar or conventional, the punch will lack impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: The bisociative point must be unmistakably double
rubrics_metrics.description: The bisociative point must be unmistakably double: the audience must recognize that the same word, image, or action genuinely fits both frames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the pivot element so that both readings are defensible and perceivable; ambiguity that favors only one frame or that yields a forced fit will fail to produce genuine bisociation.

rubrics_metrics.name: The shift from M1 to M2 must be sudden
rubrics_metrics.description: The shift from M1 to M2 must be sudden — the punch must be a switch, not a fade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid gradual or telegraphed transitions; the retroactive reinterpretation should arrive abruptly so the audience experiences cognitive 'flip' necessary for humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: An aggressive or self-assertive emotion must be present
rubrics_metrics.description: An aggressive or self-assertive emotion must be present to discharge as laughter; in humor the discharged feeling is self-assertive/aggressive (mockery, hostility, schadenfreude).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for an affective climate where the redundant energy from violated or thwarted M1 expectations can release as self-assertive emotion. If the affect is purely aesthetic or integrative, the effect will be artful or scientific rather than comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength of bisociation (strong vs weak)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong: the M1 reading was robust and seemed inevitable; the M2 reveal feels surprising yet retroactively natural. Weak: M1 was thin and easy to suspend; M2 was telegraphed; the reveal feels mechanical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether M1 genuinely committed the audience (robust expectations) and whether M2 both surprises and reframes the setup naturally. Avoid thin setups or obvious leads that produce mechanical punches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge mechanics (availability of redundant emotional energy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter results from the redundant emotional energy of the M1 expectation having nowhere to go and discharging when M2 supplants M1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing, ensure M1 builds an expectation that is emotionally invested enough to create surplus energy at the moment of sudden reinterpretation; too little investment yields little or no discharge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic questions for assessing bisociation
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of diagnostic questions: What is M1? What rules/expectations did the setup activate? What is M2? What alternative frame fits the punch? Does the bisociative element really fit both matrices? Is the shift sudden? Is the audience's emotional energy of M1 expectation now redundant and available for discharge? Is the affect of the discharge self-assertive rather than purely aesthetic?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions as a checklist when analyzing or editing a joke to ensure all components of successful comic bisociation are present and robust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional climate distinguishes humor from other bisociative forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Though science and art also rely on bisociation, they differ in the emotional climate: science yields intellectual integration (eureka), art yields participatory self-transcendent feeling (empathy, awe), while humor yields self-assertive/aggressive discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for comedy, align the emotional outcome toward self-assertion/mockery; if your bisociation produces primarily awe or intellectual satisfaction, you may be producing art or insight rather than humor.
